'''''Gentiana  villosa''''', the '''striped gentian''', is a herbaceous [[perennial plant]] belonging to the genus ''[[Gentiana]]''. It is found mainly in the Eastern United States and is used medicinally by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]] tribes.

==Description==
''Gentiana villosa'' can reach a height of two feet. The leaves are lanceolet but are typically wider above the middle of the leaf. The leaves are dark green and shiny. The flowers are clustered at the terminal bud of the plant and are white with purple stripes. ''G. villosa'' typically blooms during the fall in late August to October.<ref>[http://www.ncwildflower.org/index.php/plants/details/gentiana-villosa/ North Carolina Native Plants Society – Native Plants Gallery – Gentiana villosa – Striped Gentian<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> The flowers are pollinated by insects that are attracted to their purple stripes and nectar. ''G. villosa'' fruits during October to November. The seeds of ''G. villosa'' differ from other [[Gentian]]s because they are wingless.<ref name="plants.usda.gov">[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=GEVI5&photoID=davi3_001_avd.tif PLANTS Profile for Gentiana villosa (striped gentian) | USDA PLANTS<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

It is believed that ''G. villosa'' was misnamed because "villosa" translated in Latin means "hairy" and ''G. villosa'' actually has no hair which is known as [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nearctica.com/flowers/dtoh/gentian/Gvillos.htm |title=Nearctica - Eastern Wildflowers - Gentianaceae - Striped Gentian (Gentiana villosa)<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2010-04-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080820032813/http://www.nearctica.com/flowers/dtoh/gentian/Gvillos.htm |archive-date=2008-08-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The flowers of ''G. villosa'' make this plant easy to identify because of their defined purple stripes.

==Distribution==
''Gentiana villosa'' is found mainly in [[pine barrens]] and open woodland regions of eighteen states in the East coast regions of the United States and spanning out to the mid-east regions of the United States. The states that ''G. villosa'' can be found in are [[Alabama|AL]], [[Washington, D.C.|DC]], [[Delaware|DE]], [[Florida|FL]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|GA]], [[Indiana|IN]], [[Kentucky|KY]], [[Louisiana|LA]], [[Maryland|MD]], [[Mississippi|MS]], [[North Carolina|NC]], [[New Jersey|NJ]], [[Ohio|OH]], [[Pennsylvania|PA]], [[South Carolina|SC]], [[Tennessee|TN]], [[Virginia|VA]], [[West Virginia|WV]]. Of these eighteen states four of them [[Indiana|IN]], [[Pennsylvania|PA]], [[Ohio|OH]], and [[Maryland|MD]] have listed ''G. villosa'' as an [[endangered species]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.dnr.state.oh.us/Portals/3/Abstracts/Abstract_pdf/G/Gentiana_villosa.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2010-04-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100203165328/https://www.dnr.state.oh.us/Portals/3/Abstracts/Abstract_pdf/G/Gentiana_villosa.pdf |archive-date=2010-02-03 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Uses==
As the common name Sampson's snakeroot indicates, ''G. villosa'' is thought to aid in the relief of snakebites.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://2bnthewild.com/plants/H82.htm |title=Closed Gentian (Gentiana clausa)<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2010-04-19 |archive-date=2010-02-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100223065602/http://2bnthewild.com/plants/H82.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> In Appalachia the roots of G. villosa are carried as a charm.<ref>[http://2bnthewild.com/plants/H82.htmpdf]{{dead link|date=April 2010}}</ref> The Catawba Indians used the boiled roots as medicine to relieve back pain.<ref>[http://www.powersource.com/cherokee/herbal.html Cherokee Messenger – Native American Herbal Remedies<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723181953/http://www.powersource.com/cherokee/herbal.html |date=July 23, 2011 }}</ref>
